articles.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
articles.summary: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but has now been honoured by Bletchley Park.
articles.body:
"My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything."

From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two.

Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort.

But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers.

About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945.

After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow.

The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile.

Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939.

He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training.

"People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started."

Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads.

"I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent."

After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father.

"I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking.

He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland.

"Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing.

"One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'.

Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking.

"He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred.

After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered.

"He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled.

So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmore, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park.

The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators.

One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them.

Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that.

"When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday."

However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred.

He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'.

"You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting."

But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort.

Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe.

At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher.

Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma."

Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers."

After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper.

"I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'."

The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role.

"My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'.

"You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that."

Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker.

"I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said.

Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together.

"Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past."

Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives.

"The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised."

Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his.

"It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said.

"He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now."

articles.title: Fighting hard-to-find Lake District wildfires 'challenging'
articles.summary: Figures show some response times in Cumbria are occasionally far longer than the 15-minute target.
articles.body:
Locating wildfires reported by visitors in remote parts of the Lake District is hampered by their unfamiliarity with the landscape, the area's fire service has warned.

Cumbria Fire and Rescue Service (CFRS) met its 15-minute response target about 87% of the time this year but took 81 minutes on one call-out, according to figures obtained via a Freedom of Information request. Two in 2024 and 2025 took about 50 minutes.

CFRS group manager Scott Cameron said finding wildfires was challenging if people calling them in did not know where they were.

"When the emergency alert went out from the government, we had around 20,999 calls in the few hours after that which were giving vague areas," he said.

The government alert was issued earlier this year to warn people about the wildfire risk and alert them to a temporary ban on disposable barbecues.

While Cameron said he could not comment on the circumstances of the 81-minute response, he said the combination of location and a "transient population of tourists" could make some call-outs challenging.

"We have the Lake District in the middle of our county where not many people live," he said.

"Naturally, our control operators will send a resource to it with a general location. It might then take time to actually work out where that location is."

The figures were obtained via a Freedom of Information Request to the 47 fire and rescue services in England and Wales by the Country Land and Business Association (CLA), which is calling for more resources and equipment for fire services as the risk from wildfires grows.

The figures show Cumbria has recorded 96 wildfires so far in 2026, compared with 230 last year, 92 in 2024, 151 in 2023 and 159 in 2022.

Cameron said the county's wetter climate had helped this year as rainfall prevented vegetation becoming as dry as in other parts of the country.

But last year had seen longer dry spells and a much higher number of wildfire incidents, he said.

CFRS had invested in specialist equipment and training since the mid-2010s and was "well prepared" for tackling wildfires but additional aerial capabilities would be beneficial, Cameron said.

The service has no drones in its inventory which he said would make it easier to monitor the spread of wildfires.

Of the 29 fire services to respond to the CLA, 77% recorded more wildfires in the first half of 2026 than in the entirety of 2024.

CLA president Gavin Lane said the UK needed to "look beyond our own borders" to places like California and Australia.

"They've invested in specialist equipment, training and a much more proactive approach to managing the land, including through controlled burning," he said.

"We should be learning from this experience."

Cameron warned that, despite being well equipped and trained and with a wetter landscape than some, Cumbria remained at risk.

"The concern is definitely real," he said.

"We will try and be as prepared as possible. The climate is changing and we need to adapt to that as a service."

articles.title: Record-smashing Super Nero stars in Greenham Common exhibition
articles.summary: The motorcycle will be telling the story of racer George Brown at the place where he made history.
articles.body:
"After 60 years, Super Nero is going home."

In 1966, motorcycle racer George Brown set 11 world and 16 national speed records at former RAF station Greenham Common near Newbury, Berkshire.

Now his motorcycle Super Nero is "the star" of an exhibition at Greenham Common Control Tower until 17 December, loaned to the charity by the National Motorcycle Museum.

Tower volunteer Steve Gouldstone said they wanted to tell the story of Brown's achievements because "nobody really knew anything about it" locally.

He said the story had come through research he had been doing about speed records in general on the common.

"To our surprise we found a very small entry about George Brown's exploits which just snowballed into exhibitions and all sorts of things."

Gouldstone said the racer had come to Greenham Common as part of a small team who "were out to smash as many records as they could".

But at the age of 55, he was deemed "too old to ride a motorbike fast" by the sports regulating body at the time.

After his remarkable achievements, however, he proved there was "no real barrier to him competing in the sport that he loved and was at the peak of his capability".

"That's why we wanted to tell the story and because it was forgotten locally," Gouldstone said.

Among the guest at the launch on 2 October were Brown's son Tony, his great - grandson Jordan and top racing car designer Adrian Reynard , who was Brown's apprentice when he was just 15.

"He came and started talking about how the bike was made, repaired and how they made it go faster and faster on each improvement," Gouldstone said.

"Other visitors were just amazed at these guys that ... were still recalling the repairs they'd made to the bike back in 1966, so it was quite surreal."

He describes the Super Nero as "one of the most iconic sprint machines probably in the world".

"It's a very special bike, based on a very old British engine," Gouldstone said.

"It was then completely rebuilt by George and his brother Cliff, plus his son and his apprentice to go as fast as possible.

"It's a pleasure to have it back in Greenham where 60 years ago it ruled the world, really."

Peter Evans, a long-standing Tower guide volunteer said: "Every day we open it's great to see our visitors spend time reading our exhibitions content and having conversations about their recollections - sometimes sharing their stories with people they have only just met."

Gouldstone added several other local voluntary organisations and businesses had "all helped make this exhibition for the charity a reality".

Two plays by Newbury historian and playwright Andy Kempe - What We Had and When Nero Burned Down the Common - will be staged at the Tower between 15-17 October.

articles.title: In 1951, a Texas town of 400 residents avoided condemnation for a federal dam; 75 years later, a 90-year-old landowner and his neighbors have temporarily halted a 30-foot border wall on the same riverfront
articles.summary: Currently, there’s a battle going on in a small Texas town along the US-Mexico border.
articles.body: Currently, there’s a battle going on in a small Texas town along the US-Mexico border. Now this particular land battle has also brought a forgotten chapter of history back to life. In 1951, residents of San Ygnacio successfully persuaded the US government to spare their community from condemnation for a federal dam project. But nearly 75 years later, the town is once again resisting a major government development; this time a proposed border wall that residents fear could damage their properties and harm the river ecosystem.At the centre of the latest struggle is Joel Ruiz, a 90-year-old landowner who has spent decades living beside the Rio Grande. He also runs a small fishing business. As per reports, Ruiz, along with other residents have managed to temporarily put a break on construction after confronting contractors, examining historical property records and pursuing legal action.However, this pause is not backed by a court order.A small town with a rich historySan Ygnacio might be a small town but it comes with a remarkable history. Founded in 1830, it is among the oldest communities in Zapata County, southern Texas. Situated along the Rio Grande, across from Mexico, the town is known for its historic sandstone houses, traditional architecture and long connection with the border region.The Texas State Historical Association records that San Ygnacio was once a centre of trade and retains a distinctive collection of 19th-century sandstone buildings. Its historic district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.What state records sayAccording to the Texas State Historical Association, in the early 1950s, plans for the Falcon Dam and its reservoir threatened to submerge settlements along the river. San Ygnacio was also among them.In April 1951, hundreds of residents petitioned the government to exclude their land from condemnation proceedings. Their argument was that the town stood high enough above the reservoir's projected maximum water level to remain safe from flooding. The petition succeeded, and San Ygnacio was spared from the planned acquisition.The victory became an important part of the town's history. Now, residents are drawing on those same records and challenging another federal project.Why residents are opposing the border wallThe latest dispute concerns the US government's renewed border-wall expansion under President Donald Trump. The programme includes steel barriers and supporting border-security infrastructure intended to strengthen control along the US-Mexico border.In San Ygnacio, construction activity has raised questions about whether the government and its contractors have the necessary rights to work on this particular land as it is privately owned.The heavy machinery cleared vegetation and damaged parts of Ruiz's riverfront property. Residents also reported that construction affected trees and an irrigation line, while a steel barrier obstructed access to his boat ramp. The fishing business he had operated for years was also disrupted.The disagreement centres on land ownership. Federal authorities have maintained that construction is taking place on government-controlled land, while residents point to property records that they say establish their ownership of the disputed areas.Texas Public Radio reported in June 2026 that landowners questioned why clearing work had begun before they had signed right-of-entry agreements or the government had completed condemnation proceedings.A fight over the river, tooFor San Ygnacio's residents, the concern extends to the river. The Rio Grande is the town's sole source of drinking water, making the riverfront's future particularly important for those living there. Also, the proposed construction has also affected the area around the San Ygnacio Bird and Butterfly Sanctuary.Ruiz helped establish the sanctuary in 1973, and residents fear that the loss of vegetation and changes to the riverfront could damage the habitat they have spent decades protecting.As per reports, the Department of Homeland Security waived several federal environmental laws to accelerate border infrastructure construction. Residents and environmental advocates argue that proceeding without the usual safeguards could have lasting consequences for the river and surrounding land.The 1951 petition returns to the spotlightArchitectural conservator Frank “Chip” Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda examined property records linked to the earlier Falcon Dam dispute and found no evidence that the government had subsequently acquired the land excluded from the original condemnation.De Anda filed lawsuits alleging that the government had taken private property in violation of the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution. Following discussions involving local officials, contractors and federal representatives, construction on the disputed land was halted temporarily.Can the town win again?San Ygnacio has secured a temporary breather for now rather than a definitive victory. Whether its residents can once again persuade the government to respect their claims remains uncertain.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up freedom, president says
articles.summary: TAIPEI — Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan’s people to exist, President Lai Ching-te ⁠said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defenses is not a provocation.
articles.body: TAIPEI — Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan’s people to exist, President Lai Ching-te ⁠said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defenses is not a provocation. Democratically governed Taiwan has faced increased military and political pressure from China, which views the island as its own territory over the strong objections of the government in Taipei. Facing China’s far larger military, which is adding advanced new weapons such as stealth-fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a huge array of missiles, Taiwan is ramping up defense spending and modernising its armed forces. Peace cannot ⁠rely solely on “wishes”, Lai said outside the Presidential Office. “Taiwan cherishes peace, but ​we ⁠will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.” Taiwan’s resolve is not only a matter of its survival in the face of “authoritarian expansion”, he added. “It is about whether the international community still believes ⁠that force cannot override rules, and that the powerful cannot strip a people of their right to determine their own future.” Defense investment not ‘provocation’ China’s ⁠Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a ‌request for comment on Lai’s speech. China, which has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls the president a “separatist” and has rebuffed his offers of talks. The U.S. welcomes Lai’s commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan ‌Strait, a senior U.S. administration official said, adding, in reference to China, that “a ‌routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions.” The United States is Taiwan’s most important international backer despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Lai did not use his usual wording that neither side of the Taiwan Strait is “subordinate” to the other, but did use a phrase from Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount, saying Taiwan must become ⁠a “‘city upon a hill,’ built with courage and confidence”. Lai said his government’s increased investment in defense aimed to deter war, not provoke it. “And we are strengthening our self-defense not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity,” he told the crowd at the event, where he also watched military displays and dancing performances. “There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist.” U.S. yet to approve new arms package In 2024, shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech as president, China held war games around the island but did not do so last year. Its last war games near Taiwan were ‌in late December, following news of an $11-billion US arms deal for Taipei, the largest ever. US President Donald Trump ​has yet to approve a second package, worth $14 billion. Lai said he welcomed the United States and China managing their competition ‌through dialogue and reducing the risk of conflict and war, ⁠in what a Taiwan official told reporters was a direct response to last month’s China-US summit in Washington. But Lai ⁠urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to join forces to retain the status quo of peace and stability in the region. Taiwan’s National Day is held on the anniversary ‌of a 1911 uprising that led to ​the overthrow of China’s last imperial dynasty and the establishment of ‌the Republic of China. The Republican government fled to Taiwan in ​1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists, and the Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

articles.title: Detained! How CJP demonstration is being curtailed even before it started
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Hours before the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) planned demonstration could begin on Saturday, police action against its leaders and supporters
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Hours before the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) planned demonstration could begin on Saturday, police action against its leaders and supporters was already under way, with multiple detentions across Delhi and beyond.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convenor Saurav Das and party leader Ashutosh Ranka were detained from inside the flight after the Mumbai flight landed.Dhruv Rathee was also detained at his Gurugram residence, while CJP legal team head Ratna Singh alleged that she and three other lawyers had been detained ahead of the protest.Police also detained people attempting to reach the Jantar Mantar, with reports of action near Janpath and other parts of the capital.Over 1,600 detainedOver 1600 people have been detained across Delhi as a preventive measure ahead of the CJP protest, as authorities stepped up security and moved to prevent the gathering from taking place.More than 400 members of the Students' Federation of India (SFI) were detained in Delhi on Saturday after they began marching towards Jantar Mantar around 10 am, SFI national president Adarsh M Saji told PTI.SFI also alleged that police personnel visited HKS Surjeet Bhawan on Friday night to search for people planning to attend the protest. The building houses the SFI Central Executive Committee office.Several lawyers marching from the Supreme Court towards Jantar Mantar were also detained on Bhagwan Das Road after being stopped at police barricades. The protesters raised slogans and carried posters demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. A lawyer said police had allowed them to march for around 100 yards before stopping them.Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan and CPI(M) MP John Brittas were also detained by police following a protest outside Kerala Bhawan in New Delhi.CPI(M) general secretary M A Baby, senior party leader Brinda Karat and other CPI(M) leaders were also detained at Jantar Mantar amid the police action against protesters.Separately, Tushar Gandhi, great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was detained ahead of a protest in Mumbai in support of the CJP's agitation at Jantar Mantar, extending the demonstrations and police action beyond the national capital.The crackdown also extended beyond the national capital, with people travelling to Delhi for the demonstration reportedly intercepted at railway stations in Madhya Pradesh.At least 14 students travelling from Pune were detained at Itarsi after being taken off the Goa Express on Friday.Four CJP volunteers from Telangana had also been detained at Bhopal railway station on October 8 while travelling to Delhi for the protest.The demonstration was called by CJP to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the proposed gathering, citing security and procedural concerns.The detentions and restrictions on movement have raised questions about the extent of preventive police action ahead of a planned demonstration.The exact number of CJP supporters detained across Delhi and other states remains unclear, with reported figures covering different locations and categories of people.CJP, student leaders condemn detentionsCJP condemned the detentions, calling them an attempt to prevent its leaders from joining the protest. Founder Abhijeet Dipke criticised the police action at Delhi airport, calling it “dictatorship” after he and two other party leaders were detained.CJP co-convenor Saurav Das also hit back, saying, “Not few. A storm is coming,” in response to reports of protesters being stopped ahead of the demonstration. The party demanded the release of those detained and said the movement would continue.AISA president Neha Bora accused the authorities of undermining democratic values amid the detentions ahead of the CJP protest. “We have shown the world that a dictator hides behind the mask of democracy,” she said, criticising the police action against protesters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Four murder arrests after teenagers attacked in Stoke-on-Trent
articles.summary: A murder investigation is launched in Stoke-on-Trent after a man dies and another is seriously hurt.
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died and another suffered life-threatening injuries in Stoke-on-Trent.

A cordon remains in place on Brookhouse Road, in Meir, after police were called to reports of violence at 23:45 BST on Friday.

A man in his late teens was confirmed dead at the scene, Staffordshire Police said, and another man, also in his late teens, was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical but stable condition.

Two 18-year-old men, a 20-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, all from Stoke-on-Trent, were arrested on suspicion of murder, while the boy was also arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. All remain in police custody.

"This is a devastating time for all those affected by what has happened overnight," said Det Insp Katie Gregory.

She added: "I'd like to reassure the community that there is no wider risk to them, and we are doing all we can to understand the circumstances that led to this tragic incident."

The force has urged anyone with information about the attack to contact police.

articles.title: ‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has pulled out all the stops to prevent Cockroach movement protests.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – Heavy police barricades line the streets around Connaught Place, the colonial-era square near Jantar Mantar, on Saturday morning as police have begun detaining groups of protesters arriving for planned demonstrations.

They are here in support of the influential Gen-Z movement and Cockroach Janta Party, which have called for the resignation of India’s election chief, amid a bitter dispute over who gets to vote in the world’s most populous democracy.

Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and a rollback of a controversial voter revision exercise which has struck 130 million names from the voter list.

For now, an eerie silence hangs over parts of central New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has gone to lengths to turn the city into a fortress, deploying nearly 30,000 personnel onto the streets.

Police ⁠have also detained the founder of ⁠the Cockroach Janta Party, Abhijeet Dipke.

Indian TV channels reported early on Saturday that officers met Dipke at New Delhi airport ⁠after he arrived ⁠from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call ⁠off the protest as authorities ⁠had banned it.

CJP leaders ⁠Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight ‌upon landing, the movement said in a statement.

On Friday, the government extraordinarily cancelled all trains to New Delhi; locked down more than 50 metro stations; imposed an internet shutdown; and sent personnel to thousands of students in local communities to warn them against participation in the protest.

Several students en route to New Delhi from different states of India were dragged out of trains and buses and detained by the police. Many have been placed under house arrest in cities hundreds of kilometres away from New Delhi.

The Cockroach movement says thousands have been detained across India as Modi’s government intensifies its crackdown. Yet undeterred protesters have pledged to keep returning to the streets.

Current restrictions in the Indian capital and the nationwide crackdown on protesters have evoked memories of the 1975 Emergency, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties, censored the press and jailed political opponents.

“Narendra Modi just made EMERGENCY official,” Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, wrote in a post on X. “This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you.”

Neha Bora, the firebrand Gen-Z protest leader and the national president of the left student body All India Students’ Association, equated the Modi government with British colonialist forces that unsuccessfully clamped down on India’s independence movement. She called on the masses to join the protest.

On Saturday morning, young people were trying to respond to her call despite the police restrictions in place.

Santosh Kumar, 29, a street sweeper in the outer circle of Connaught Place, told Al Jazeera he feels frustrated seeing teenagers detained at police barricades.

“How can you stop these kids? They are detaining 10; 50 more are coming. Modi, the dictator’s time is up: He will not even stay until 2029 (the time of the next elections).

“This is the time we turn Delhi into Nepal and Bangladesh – learn from them and take back our country,” he said, referring to youth-led movements in those countries.

Sameer Irshad, 28, an engineer from Gurugram, approached the barricades near Connaught Place while pushing his 57-year-old mother Sheeba Abdi in a wheelchair.

Abdi told us: “This sort of crackdown, where we cannot peacefully express our dissent, is unseen in Delhi. Why has government turned this place into a fortress? Why are they so scared of citizens like me?”

Last month, India was shaken by revelations of divisions within the supposedly autonomous body that is in charge of conducting elections, over controversial policies that critics say have disenfranchised tens of millions of people.

India’s Election Commission chief, Gyanesh Kumar, was accused of overruling concerns raised by the two other election commissioners about the integrity of ongoing changes in the voter database, an investigation by The Indian Express reported.

India is among the few countries to have taken an active approach to enrolling every last voter.

Critics say the ongoing revision of the voter list flips the foundational principle of Indian democracy: Demanding that citizens prove their voting rights, and disproportionately targeting Muslims, economically weaker sections, minorities and other vulnerable groups in Indian society.

Arif, a 24-year-old district coordinator for the Students’ Federation of India, another left-wing student organisation to have joined the protest call, was locked in his home in Saharanpur, nearly 200km (125 miles) from New Delhi, on Thursday.

“Several police officials started beating my door out of nowhere late at night, asking my parents for details of my whereabouts,” Arif, who did not want to give his full name, told Al Jazeera from his home in Saharanpur, where he is currently detained under the police’s watch around the clock.

“They just want to stop me from going to Delhi for protest. They are threatening to book me under criminal cases and destroy my future,” he said, adding that this is the first time he has been subject to such detention.

“I really wanted to be in Delhi, to fight and reclaim our democracy. The time for Modi is over,” he said.

This week, Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BNP) celebrated his 25 years in office, starting with his years as chief minister of the western state of Gujarat – where he oversaw the infamous 2002 Muslim pogrom – and later as India’s prime minister since 2014.

But Modi has never looked weaker in power than now, analysts and Indian political observers argue.

In July, the Cockroach-led protests choked key New Delhi streets and forced out Modi’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

This time, Modi has taken more extreme measures to prevent protesters from gaining a foothold in central New Delhi, “because he wishes to retain the aura and image of a leader who never yields to public pressure, someone who is invincible”, said Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an author and biographer of Modi.

“Modi appears at the lowest point [of his political life] in public perception. This is extremely paradoxical because he has some of the most important autonomous institutions, large sections of the bureaucracy, and state wings in tight control and acting at his behest,” Mukhopadhyay told Al Jazeera.

In the face of growing protests, Modi is now “fast losing people’s perception of being a leader who leads them out of livelihood pits”, he said.

Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court and a rights activist who planned to join the protest on Saturday, told Al Jazeera that “Modi’s government looks quite scared of the people.

“People in India are rising and demanding answers. And when the government gets scared, they adopt draconian measures to stay in power,” Bhushan said. “But only more and more people will rise from repression.”

articles.summary: John Paul DeJoria, co-founder of John Paul Mitchell Systems and Patrón Spirits, has sold Patrón de Paz, his ranch in Dripping Springs, Texas, for $6.93
articles.body: John Paul DeJoria, co-founder of John Paul Mitchell Systems and Patrón Spirits, has sold Patrón de Paz, his ranch in Dripping Springs, Texas, for $6.93 million. The property covers roughly 96 acres, about 25 miles outside Austin, and includes a four-bedroom main house of about 7,500 square feet, a swimming pool and two barns. About 120 exotic animals, among them wildebeest, oryx, gazelle and antelope, were included in the price. The ranch also has a 2,700-square-foot underground bomb shelter stocked with food and water. The buyer, Austin-based television producer Jonathan Nowzaradan, plans to move there.How much did John Paul sell his 96-acre Texas estate forAccording to The Wall Street Journal, DeJoria sold the ranch for $6.93 million, a figure given by listing agent Dave Murray. The ranch is named Patron de Paz after DeJoria's liquor company. The property was sold fully furnished. The Journal reports that the ranch first went on the market in 2015 for $7.995 million, and the price was later reduced to $7.495 million. Murray, of the DMTX Realty Group at Coldwell Banker United, held the listing together with Gregg Sellers of Horizon Realty.According to the Journal, the ranch covers roughly 96 acres in Dripping Springs, a suburb about 25 miles outside Austin. Public records, the newspaper says, show that DeJoria bought the property in October 2008. The main house has four bedrooms and measures about 7,500 square feet. The grounds include a swimming pool and two barns, each with housing for caretakers.What exotic animals lived on billionaire John’s 96-acre Texas estateThe ranch is home to about 120 exotic animals, including wildebeest, oryx, gazelle and antelope. Murray told the newspaper that the animals were included in the sale price. The buyer is Jonathan Nowzaradan, an Austin-based television producer, who told the Journal he plans to move to the ranch. He described the experience of living there as feeling "like you're on an African safari."DeJoria also built a 2,700-square-foot underground bomb shelter. The three-bedroom space is stocked with food and water. Nowzaradan told the newspaper that the space could be used as a game room or for other purposes. DeJoria co-founded the hair products company John Paul Mitchell Systems in 1980 and went on to become one of the creators of Patrón, a premium tequila company. articles.title: A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
articles.summary: The football club founded in a West Bank refugee camp has built a global movement of solidarity.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Nearly 200 people packed into Edami, a small Lebanese bakery in east London, to celebrate a decade of Lajee Celtic, a grassroots sports club based in a Palestinian refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.

What began as a football project has grown into an international symbol of solidarity.

In London, the room was filled with Palestinian flags, the aroma of Edami’s freshly baked manousheh, and Lajee Celtic shirts – which have been worn by celebrities, including football icon Eric Cantona and the actor Hannah Einbinder.

Martin, a Lajee Celtic organiser, travelled down from Glasgow for the celebration in September. He first visited Aida Camp, in the occupied West Bank, more than 10 years ago, a trip he described as life-changing.

“I don’t think anyone would really have expected that the project would have been as successful as it’s been,” said Martin, who requested to be identified by his first name. “But Celtic is a unique football club with its foundation, its Irish identity, the diaspora community, its universal support and then the values, which tie so much of that together.”

The relationship between Aida Camp, where Lajee is based, and Celtic supporters developed over years.

Mohammed al-Azzeh, director of the Lajee Centre, which provides services to the youth of the camp, remembers how it all began.

“We’d built up relationships with friends from Scotland and Ireland who had visited Palestine, and then in 2012, I travelled to Glasgow for the first time. We started to have conversations about creating a football academy,” he recalled.

By 2015, the idea was taking shape when a group of footballers from the camp travelled to Belfast to play a game.

Then came the 2016 Champions League draw. Celtic were paired with Israeli side Hapoel Be’er Sheva.

Supporters ignored warnings that displaying Palestinian flags could result in a fine. As the teams emerged, the stadium was transformed into a sea of Palestinian flags, an action led by Celtic ultras, the Green Brigade.

The Green Brigade responded by launching the Match The Fine For Palestine campaign. Not to pay the fine, but to support Palestinian organisations, including with the formation of a football academy in Aida Camp.

“The support and solidarity shown in that game was really a pivotal moment,” he said. “And that’s what ultimately led to Lajee Celtic becoming what it is today.”

The team has brought together young Palestinians from villages around Bethlehem, refugee camps and communities in Hebron and Jerusalem.

“It means a lot, for us as Palestinians, to be in one place and meeting each other,” al-Azzeh said. “It becomes about more than just playing football.”

Lajee Celtic is competing in organised football for the first time. The club had been due to enter the Palestinian league three years ago, but the competition was cancelled when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began. Now, despite restrictions on movement between Palestinian cities and the wider disruption to football, the club has entered the Thousand Martyrs Cup, named after the 1,014 athletes killed in Gaza since October 2023.

Bassil Mikdadi, journalist and founder of Football Palestine, said that international reach has given Lajee Celtic a significance beyond the club itself.

“Lajee Celtic is a blueprint for ways in which fans of European clubs can directly support those on the ground in Palestine. It’s connective tissue,” he said.

For Martin, the popular shirts are more than merchandise.

“When people buy these shirts, they do so knowing that the money is funding football, sports and general youth development in Palestine. And then when the same people wear these shirts, whether they’re in Glasgow or London or New York, they’re each making their own individual solidarity action.”

Lajee Celtic created a link between clubs and communities inside Palestine and supporters and campaigners abroad.

“It has this kind of cross-cultural, cross-border solidarity,” he said.

That connection has become increasingly important as Palestinian football has struggled to continue since the genocide in Gaza.

For Mikdadi, the survival of grassroots clubs is essential: They are the groundwork for the national team.

“The success of the Palestinian national team in recent years … the base of that success has always been players provided by clubs in the West Bank and Gaza,” he said.

The club’s ambitions stretch beyond football. It has expanded into sports such as boxing and table tennis, while creating opportunities for young Palestinians across Palestine and the diaspora.

“Fundraising campaigns come and go all the time. But when you create a football club and when you have that sort of tangible idea at the heart of it, then you are creating a journey,” said Martin.

Mohammed al-Azzeh recalled a meaningful memory on a beach in Cape Town, South Africa, where the team played two friendlies in 2025.

Samir al-Amir, a coordinator with Lajee Celtic, had spent more than 19 years in Israeli prisons. When he travelled with the team to South Africa, it was the first time he had been able to leave the walls and checkpoints of the West Bank.

Al-Azzeh remembers watching him on the beach.

“He was acting like a young boy because it was the first time seeing the sea,” he said. “Without Lajee Celtic, I’m not sure Samir would have ever had that opportunity. That illustrates why the project is so important,” he said.

articles.title: Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane
articles.summary: More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama have been left without power as Isaias downs trees, power lines.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias has crashed into the United States Gulf Coast before losing speed and turning into a post-tropical storm as it moved over southern Alabama, threatening flash flooding and strong winds farther inland.

The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Saturday that Isaias is about 89km (55 miles) south-southwest of Montgomery, with maximum ⁠sustained winds of 100 kilometres per hour (65 ⁠miles per hour).

When it made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), the agency said.

Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways.

While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.

Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended their emergency response on Friday night because of dangerous conditions.

Parts of southern Alabama were also flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines.

Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.

More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.

One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could reach 0.91-1.52 metres (3-5ft) from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Florida’s Aucilla River, according to the hurricane centre.

The storm grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights in and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport.

Asked about hurricane preparations, President Donald Trump ⁠told reporters outside the White House, “We’re watching it very ⁠closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control”.

Florida’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, with search-and-rescue teams ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.

“Emergency declarations have ‌been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X, as residents ‌were urged to take shelter and watch out for hurricane conditions.

Another tropical storm, Rachel, was also expected to bring strong winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

And Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrelled towards Mexico’s coast early on Saturday.

The NHC said Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 225km/h (140mph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane.

Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along the coast of Jalisco and in parts of Michoacan, Colima, and Nayarit.

Forecasters warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

articles.title: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
articles.summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman wanted to make his kingdom a magnet for investment, tourism and the world’s biggest sporting events. Now drones and missiles launched from Yemen are slamming into Saudi cities, drawing the kingdom deeper into the regional turmoil he hoped to leave behind.
articles.body: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman wanted to make his kingdom a magnet for investment, tourism and the world’s biggest sporting events. Now drones and missiles launched from Yemen are slamming into Saudi cities, drawing the kingdom deeper into the regional turmoil he hoped to leave behind. The civil war in Yemen erupted once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, breaking years of relative calm. Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Iran-allied Houthi group, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Iran. Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say. Saudi Arabia’s ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged President Donald Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis in Yemen. Now, Riyadh is trying to regain its footing by supporting its Yemeni partners in yet another campaign against the Houthis, an operation named “Yemen’s Dawn.” Prince Mohammed’s ambitions to transform his kingdom have already faced several challenges since his rise to power more than a decade ago. Today, they’re coming under further strain as multi-front attacks on oil infrastructure cut into exports, major projects are canceled, and the kingdom is pulled into a war with no clear way out. At least three people, including a Saudi pilot, were killed this week after Houthi forces struck several airports in the kingdom, according to Saudi Arabia. Regional turmoil has forced the suspension of star-studded film festivals, award shows, and music concerts this year. Meanwhile, the kingdom’s flagship financial conference, which is expected to draw high-profile business leaders at the end of October, is coming under pressure amid the strikes. “They just needed the conflict to stay (as) far away from them as possible without the Houthis disrupting their transformation plans,” Michael Ratney, the former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told CNN. “Now they find themselves in the middle of it.” A hasty UAE exit When Saudi warplanes struck a shipment of military vehicles sent to Yemen by the UAE last year, a decade-old alliance between two nations fighting Iran’s influence in Yemen shattered, leaving the kingdom to contend with the crisis alone after Abu Dhabi withdrew its forces. The break with the UAE shocked the region. Saudi Arabia launched a rare media campaign against its neighbor, accusing it of fueling instability in Sudan and Yemen. Saudi commentators publicly cast the UAE as a younger sibling rebelling against a wiser one. Saudi Arabia is the “head and body” on which regional stability rests, wrote prominent Saudi journalist Dawood Al-Shirian in January. “If (Saudi Arabia) stumbles, the entire system is disrupted and the Gulf scatters.” As Riyadh pressed for dominance in the Gulf, the ground shifted in Yemen. The four-year ceasefire with the Houthis was already fragile, and the rapid UAE withdrawal as demanded by Riyadh left thousands of fighters who had spent a decade under Abu Dhabi’s command disoriented by Riyadh’s strategy. Fighters allied with the UAE say Abu Dhabi’s departure left a power vacuum the Saudis didn’t fill. “There wasn’t a proper transition when the Emiratis left,” a southern Yemeni official, who asked to remain anonymous to speak freely to CNN, said. “It was frightening how different things became. The Emiratis’ command and control was very efficient, and the Saudis did not replace this efficiency.” CNN reached out to the Saudi government for comment on whether the forces fighting the Houthis on the ground received enough support and whether there was a proper transition. Lack of preparation Eight weeks after the UAE withdrawal, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The moves sparked a conflict that has plunged the region into unprecedented turmoil and placed Washington’s allies, including Saudi Arabia, in Iran’s crosshairs. The timing was unfortunate for Saudi Arabia, several experts say. After contending with the UAE-backed separatist push in Yemen, the US and Israel triggered a regional war. And despite years of trying to stop the war from breaking out in Yemen, the pressure Trump imposed on Iran was expected to eventually trigger a Houthi push on the kingdom. “The Saudis had to respond after being attacked by an enemy force on their territory… so there was always going to be a response,” Ratney, the former US ambassador, said. Even as Iranian missiles struck the kingdom from the east, Saudi attention focused on the south. The Houthis, still formally in a truce with Riyadh, appeared unwilling to aid their Iranian partners. Tehran instead drew the Saudis in. In July, Iran sent a commercial plane to carry a Houthi delegation to Khamenei’s funeral in Tehran, defying a Saudi air blockade of Yemen. Riyadh struck the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa to prevent the plane from landing. The rebel group retaliated by declaring the truce dead and announced a naval blockade on Saudi ships. It also started a lightning offensive down Yemen’s coast, seizing strategic territory at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the largest escalation since 2022. The Houthis attacked Saudi oil facilities and pipelines, disrupting crude supplies and sending prices sharply higher. Saudi forces answered with hundreds of airstrikes. “The Saudis have made several mistakes and failures,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen with the International Crisis Group think tank, told CNN, noting that Riyadh hadn’t prepared for a Houthi offensive and lacked coordination with allied Yemeni forces it inherited from the UAE. “The areas they’ve lost created morale issues with their allies and now it’s a big challenge for the Saudis as the Houthis have more advanced weaponry which managed to reach several cities in Saudi Arabia,” he said. ‘Unpredictable’ Trump Another miscalculation by Saudi Arabia was its reliance on continued American support, experts say. Despite signing a new defense pact with Washington last year and being designated a Major Non-NATO Ally by the US, Riyadh has been disappointed by what it sees as waning US commitment to its security. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month, urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but Trump declined to intervene. Washington instead met the Houthis in Oman, seeking to protect its own ceasefire with the group, which made it clear that its war was with Saudi Arabia alone, thus allowing US vessels to traverse the Red Sea freely. For a military that has built its “entire worldview” around partnering with the US, the Saudis are realizing how unpredictable Trump is, said Ratney. “It was never their concept or the structure of their military to fight these wars by themselves,” he said. “Under a normal US presidency, if something like this happens, we would’ve helped our partner in what would’ve been a rational and considered process. “Now we don’t have that process, and it ultimately comes down to: what does Trump think? And the Saudis probably feel exposed as a result,” he added. Saudi Arabia has since looked elsewhere. Last month, Prince Mohammed flew to Egypt to meet President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, then invited UAE Vice President Sheik Mansour bin Zayed to Riyadh a few weeks later to discuss regional developments. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel. Britain said it would send an aircraft to help refuel Saudi jets. More than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed on Monday to “activate collective deterrence measures” under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement after an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The pact, set up earlier this year, is meant to coordinate defense and security cooperation among the three. Forces loyal to the UAE also appear to be taking part in the offensive, a sign of at least a partial thaw between the kingdom and the UAE. A regional solution But experts warn that outside support and early gains by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government will not settle the conflict. Infighting remains common among the factions, and there is still no clear political end state. A sustained push against Iranian-backed forces, analysts say, would require organization, regional backing, funding, and logistics that the current coalition has not yet shown it can sustain. “They need to unify their command centers, they need to resolve the issues they have between the various factions within the group,” Hisham Al Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser for the European Institute of Peace told CNN’s Becky Anderson. “Territorial gains they’ve made would mean nothing if the (Saudi-backed) Yemeni government cannot maintain control over those areas.” Many experts said however that the fighting in Yemen is connected to the US war in Iran, and as long as the conflict between Washington and Tehran is ongoing, the Iranians will continue having a powerful incentive to watch the Houthis disrupt Saudi Arabia. Gulf states could manage to secure a separate diplomatic solution with Iran, analysts say, or escalate their military strikes to eliminate Houthi leadership. “Neither of those scenarios fix the conflict in Yemen in any near term,” Ratney said. “The Saudis will have to just figure out an imperfect path ahead.”

articles.title: Journalist Hamurabi Huesca Manzano killed in Mexico’s Oaxaca
articles.summary: Conflicting reports emerge on the circumstances of the killing, prompting calls for justice from advocacy groups.
articles.body:
A journalist moonlighting as a taxi driver has been shot dead in the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, the ninth killed in the country this year, according to human rights organisation Article 19.

Hamurabi Huesca Manzano, who owned the news website Pinotepa Comunica, was killed on Friday after an armed group opened fire on him and two others, according to the state prosecutor’s report.

The office said one line of inquiry suggests that a dispute happened between local criminal groups, and that the intended target of the shooting was a man known as “El Dario”.

El Dario, infamous for instigating violence on the Oaxaca coast, was wounded in the shooting and died in hospital hours later. According to prosecutors, Huesca Manzano was working as a taxi driver, waiting to take El Dario somewhere else when the journalist was shot dead.

The prosecutor’s office says the attackers have been “fully identified”, but did not name them or say whether Huesca Manzano’s journalistic work played any role.

Local reports give differing accounts of where the attack happened, as well; a number of them say Huesca Manzano was shot at his home and that a woman was also injured.

Article 19 condemned the killing and said on X: “We demand that the prosecutor’s office treat his journalistic work as a priority in its investigation.”

The mayor of San Miguel Tlacamama, Antonio Olmedo Mendoza, confirmed Manzano’s death and offered condolences in a statement, local media reported.

“With deep sorrow, I regret the passing of Hamurabi Sinclair Huesca Manzano,” he said, adding that he joined the grief of his family, friends and colleagues.

Mexico is notorious for being one of the most dangerous countries for journalists, with more than 150 media workers killed there since 1994, according to Reporters Without Borders.

articles.title: France is devouring itself as school riots reveal a crisis far bigger than broken classrooms
articles.summary: France student protests over crumbling schools expose deep tensions as Jean-Luc Mélenchon's La France Insoumise allegedly exploits the growing unrest.
articles.body: Student protests over crumbling schools despite billions in public spending are fueling a broader crisis in France, as experts warn that the country's mounting financial troubles, President Emmanuel Macron's weakened political center and radical movements are pushing the unrest far beyond its original educational grievances. Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' senior envoy for Europe, told Fox News Digital in an interview from Paris that what began in September with legitimate complaints about school conditions has increasingly been exploited by political forces seeking confrontation with the state. "Overall I'd say the anger is real but the violence I would say is organized," she said, adding that destroying schools would do nothing to improve the education system. FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION Seventy-two percent of education expenditure went toward salaries, social contributions and pensions for teaching and non-teaching personnel, while just 8.5% went toward investment, including infrastructure and equipment. The figures cover the entire education system, not just high schools, according to France's Education Ministry's 2026 statistical overview. Harvey Feigenbaum, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University and an expert on French politics, told Fox News Digital that France's underlying problem is a government caught between expensive social commitments, sluggish economic growth and mounting pressure to cut spending. "France is in deep debt. It wants to cut its expenses," Feigenbaum said, explaining that years of financial pressure and neglected school facilities have fueled frustration among students. The scale of the financial predicament is striking. According to Eurostat, French public debt stood at 117.6% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, the third-highest ratio in the European Union, behind Greece and Italy. Reuters reported October 8 that rising borrowing costs and investor concerns have severely limited the government's ability to resolve unrest through additional spending, a strategy employed during previous waves of French protests. The financial squeeze has collided with an increasingly fragmented political system, creating opportunities for parties at both ends of the political spectrum to capitalize on public dissatisfaction. FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’ Macron's political center collapses For Feigenbaum, the long-term roots of the crisis lie in Macron's political legacy. When Macron won the presidency in 2017, he promised to move beyond France's traditional left-right divide, combining policies from both sides into a new centrist political movement. But Feigenbaum argues that the strategy produced an unintended consequence: weakening France's established moderate parties without creating a durable governing coalition to replace them. "What he ended up doing was attracting the moderate voters from the parties of the moderate left and the parties from the moderate right, and essentially destroyed those parties," Feigenbaum said. He argued that the collapse of the traditional political center helped create space for more ideologically polarized movements. "Macron is a smart man, but he's a terrible politician," the professor added. Macron's controversial pension reforms illustrate the difficulty of persuading French voters to accept reductions in longstanding public benefits, Feigenbaum argued. Those efforts triggered widespread protests, while implementation of the 2023 retirement changes has since been suspended until 2028. The situation became especially difficult after Macron called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, producing a deeply divided National Assembly without a governing majority. "Even if the government wanted to do something coherent, they simply don't have the votes to do it," Feigenbaum said. That paralysis has left Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu handling the immediate unrest while Macron faces questions about the stability of the political system he helped reshape. FRENCH PM REJECTS POLICE BRUTALITY CLAIMS AFTER TEENS SEVERELY INJURED IN PROTESTS: 'ACCIDENTS HAPPEN' Why are France's schools struggling despite billions in spending? The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September amid complaints about overcrowded classrooms, inadequate heating and cooling, aging buildings and teachers who were not replaced when absent. Rodan-Benzaquen said the anger reflected years of educational instability, frequent ministerial changes and reforms that have failed to resolve persistent school problems. She also pointed to a broader sense of anxiety among young people about their economic future, artificial intelligence, climate change and international conflicts. According to the OECD's September 2026 Education at a Glance report, France spent $16,674 in funding per student in general upper-secondary education in 2023, compared with an OECD average of $12,421, adjusted for purchasing power. Yet teachers and students continue to complain about basic shortages. Responsibility for public high school buildings and equipment falls to regional authorities, while the national government oversees much of the education system, including teacher staffing. Feigenbaum said France's centralized education structure makes national leaders the focus of public anger when schools fail to deliver. The pressure has already forced a concession. Reuters reported Friday that Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced an emergency plan to deploy 3,000 qualified educators to particularly affected schools, costing several dozen million euros. Student unions welcomed the measure as an initial victory but pledged to continue demonstrating. The spending figures raise broader questions about whether France's financial and political priorities have left sufficient resources for maintaining school infrastructure and meeting students' needs. They do not, however, establish that teachers' unions or other organized constituencies have improperly diverted funding. TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT How the far left entered the unrest As the demonstrations expanded, the involvement of France's hard-left La France Insoumise party, known as LFI, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, became an increasingly contentious issue. Reuters reported October 1 that French intelligence agencies had told a government crisis meeting that LFI and affiliated activists played a role in fomenting the unrest. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also cited agitators moving between schools to encourage violence. LFI has denied responsibility and accused authorities of aggravating tensions through their response. Rodan-Benzaquen said far-left movements were capitalizing on students' frustration. "There is an obvious instrumentalization, obvious manipulation," she said, arguing that activists were seeking to push some protesters toward violence. She linked the unrest to what she described as Mélenchon's broader political strategy ahead of France's 2027 presidential election. "His idea is that on the one hand he will scare voters on the right and on the far right, who will then go to vote for the far-right, and on the other hand he would mobilize his own camp," she said. Rodan-Benzaquen argued that intensifying political confrontation could help Mélenchon consolidate his support among younger voters and immigrant communities, while portraying the far right as an increasingly serious threat. She described it as a calculated political strategy rather than a spontaneous response to students' concerns. The involvement of LFI politicians has been documented by French media, although there is disagreement over whether the party helped initiate the demonstrations or became involved after the protests began. An October 2 investigation by Le Monde examined a police intelligence assessment describing radical-left activity around schools in Seine-Saint-Denis but questioned whether the evidence established that the movement itself was politically orchestrated. Feigenbaum offered a more cautious interpretation, describing some of the violent perpetrators as fringe provocateurs who exploit broader demonstrations without necessarily directing them. "They're not being organized by some, you know, some mastermind at the national level, at least as far as anyone knows," he said. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE Islamist influence or political solidarity? The demonstrations have also raised questions about whether Islamist groups and pro-Palestinian activists are seeking to use the unrest to advance broader ideological causes. Rodan-Benzaquen argued that Mélenchon's emphasis on Gaza and the Palestinian cause has helped bring together political constituencies that might otherwise have little in common. "It's sort of the idea of sort of an intersection of different movements where they manage to bring together the different groups, the far left, Islamist movements, pro-Palestinian activists," she said. She pointed to Palestinian flags appearing during the demonstrations as an indication of how the movement has expanded beyond its original educational demands. The FDD expert argued that Islamist elements were attempting to capitalize on the turmoil, although she cautioned against reducing the entire crisis to immigration or religion. "But this goes far beyond the issue of immigration, it goes far beyond the issue of Islamism, it goes far beyond the issue of Islam," she said. EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT A crisis France cannot simply spend its way out of The government's latest concessions have not ended the protests. According to Reuters on Friday, 141 schools remained closed while students continued demanding broader reforms. Nearly 10% of teaching hours in French public high schools remained unstaffed. For Rodan-Benzaquen, one of the greatest dangers is that the demonstrations reflect a society increasingly divided into competing political realities. She described how her 17-year-old son created separate left-wing and right-wing Instagram accounts and encountered radically different portrayals of the same unrest: one emphasizing police violence and the other violence by protesters. "Now, if you live in two drastically different realities, it is very complicated to come to any form of dialog and end agreement," she said. Her warning extends beyond France's current protests. "We are in an extremely polarized environment," Rodan-Benzaquen said, noting that social media can deepen divisions and allow confrontations to escalate rapidly. Feigenbaum sees an additional structural danger: a government burdened by accumulated financial obligations and deprived of the political consensus needed to reform them. The result is a country spending heavily to sustain its public institutions while struggling to deliver the services citizens expect — and a political system increasingly consumed by conflict over how to fix them. articles.title: A 3D-printed bridge inspired by Leonardo da Vinci uses waste stone and marble powder; 13 printed blocks form a self-supporting structure
articles.summary: A bridge inspired by a design sketched by Leonardo da Vinci more than 500 years ago has been brought to life as a modern prototype using 3D printing and
articles.body: A bridge inspired by a design sketched by Leonardo da Vinci more than 500 years ago has been brought to life as a modern prototype using 3D printing and waste from stone processing. WASP and the Polytechnic University of Bari said, the project team describes Da Vinci's Bridge as the first 3D-printed bridge to use waste materials from stone processing , combining additive manufacturing with Leonardo's original vision for a self-supporting structure. The project was conceived by Professor Giuseppe Fallacara of the Polytechnic University of Bari and draws on Leonardo's design for a bridge that would have connected the Pera district, present-day Galata in Beyoğlu, with Constantinople, today's Istanbul, across the Golden Horn. The prototype is a pedestrian bridge with a span of approximately 6 metres and adapts Leonardo's concept for the needs of the experiment.Da Vinci's Bridge: how 3D printing brings Leonardo's design into the modern eraThe project's distinctive feature is not simply that the bridge was 3D-printed, but that its construction material incorporates waste from stone and marble processing. B&Y, an Italian start-up led by Vincenzo Gurrado, developed a low-environmental-impact mortar made from 30% waste stone and marble powders combined with a lime-based binder. The project brought together the ArCoD department of the Polytechnic University of Bari with WASP, which supplied the 3D-printing technology, and B&Y, which developed the material. The project demonstrates how waste generated during stone processing can be incorporated into a material for 3D-printed construction rather than being treated solely as a disposal problem.Leonardo's original bridge was never built, but its design was notable for its self-supporting form. The modern project does not reproduce the proposed structure at its original scale. Instead, Fallacara's team adapted the concept into a roughly 6-metre pedestrian prototype, allowing the researchers to test the combination of 3D printing, stone-processing waste and the geometric principles behind Leonardo's design.Inside the material: mortar made with 30% waste stone and marble powdersTurning the material into a physical bridge required large-format 3D printing. WASP provided its machines and technical expertise for producing the blocks that form the structure. The bridge was divided into 13 blocks with variable layers, each printed using the WASP 3MT LDM Concrete, a large-format printer designed for cementitious materials. The printed blocks were then assembled by the University of Bari using a system of temporary centering, which supported the pieces during construction.Once the blocks were assembled, the temporary supports could be removed. The completed structure is able to support itself through the principle of stereotomy, which was also central to Leonardo's original bridge concept. In this approach, the geometry and arrangement of individual structural pieces allow them to work together as a self-supporting whole. The project therefore combines a historical construction principle with a contemporary manufacturing process rather than simply reproducing Leonardo's drawing in a different material.Stereotomy and self-support: how 13 printed blocks form the bridgeThe use of stereotomy is key to the bridge's structure. Leonardo's original design relied on the arrangement of individual elements to create a self-supporting form, and the modern prototype applies the same underlying principle to its 13 3D-printed blocks. The temporary centring system was used during assembly, but the finished bridge does not depend on those temporary supports to remain standing.
