articles.title: ‘Donroe’ Doctrine and conservative victories squeeze cartels in Latin America
articles.summary: The Sinaloa cartel and CJNG are rapidly adapting as Trump's Shield of the Americas coalition squeezes drug trafficking routes across the hemisphere.
articles.body: The cartels are losing political cover, and they know it. The Trump administration has treated the Western Hemisphere as a security problem — rather than allow diplomatic courtesy to block needed action. Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro is in U.S. custody. Colombia elected Abelardo de la Espriella, who ran against negotiations with armed groups and won. Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Paraguay and others have aligned with Washington’s enforcement policies. The Shield of the Americas coalition now coordinates intelligence and operations against cartel networks – but with a handful of exceptions: Mexico, Brazil, Cuba and Nicaragua. That is the Donroe Doctrine in practice: American predominance in the hemisphere, applied to migration, Chinese footholds and the drug trade. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY Critically, this is a major shift in the operating environments for the Sinaloa cartel, CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), and the Colombian and Venezuelan networks that fed them. Cuba is the weakest link in the old arc. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the regime has already fallen as a functioning state. About a fifth of the population has left since 2021. The lights fail, the peso is worthless and the government that remains specializes in jailing people. Whether the Castro apparatus collapses by December is unknowable. What is knowable is that Havana is no longer a reliable logistics or intelligence partner for anyone who needs one. In Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Morena government is increasingly alone. It keeps bilateral contacts with Washington while refusing the regional coalition, citing fear of U.S. operations on Mexican soil. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins the Brazilian runoff, Sheinbaum’s remaining major left-of-center counterpart in the region is gone. Isolation raises the diplomatic cost of open sanctuary to the drug lords. But the cartels are already adjusting. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN In August, Spanish police rolled up a CJNG-linked cell that moved roughly 2.5 tons of methamphetamine dissolved in vanilla aroma and finished it in a lab in Lleida. Earlier Sinaloa shipments concealed in marble statues met the same end. Mexican groups are treating Europe as a synthetics market precisely because cocaine corridors face more hostile governments. Colombia’s new president has ended the prior administration’s accommodation with armed actors. Venezuelan airspace and ports, long protected by the Cartel de los Soles network, are under direct U.S. pressure. U.S. strikes on drug running fast boats have sharply reduced Eastern Caribbean drug traffic. Routes move. Chemistry is portable — coca fields aren’t. TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT Violence is scaling with the same logic. Mexican authorities have arrested clusters of former Colombian soldiers — nine of 12 in one Michoacán case were ex-military — after mine attacks that killed Mexican troops. These men are hired for ambush drills, explosives and drone work. They are not a kill team loyal to former Colombian President Gustavo Petro; Petro is out of office. They are mercenaries. Cartels pay for skills the Mexican state has not matched. The drone piece is further along than most reporting admits. Cartel explosives drops from commercial quadcopters are already routine. French and U.S. defense outlets have documented Mexican and Colombian nationals entering Ukraine’s International Legion, some with fraudulent papers, seeking assignment to First-Person View (FPV) units. One alias, Águila-7, drew instructor suspicion in Lviv for technical proficiency inconsistent with a humanitarian volunteer. The skills learned on a brutal battlefield transfer seamlessly to the Western Hemisphere. CRIME, KIDNAPPINGS AND DRONE ATTACKS FLAGGED IN US WARNING FOR BORDER REGION And a prosecutor’s office in Tijuana has already been hit by nail-packed drones. Border sightings run into the tens of thousands. The February El Paso airspace closure was the public admission of a problem that has been operational for years. In Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Morena government is increasingly alone. It keeps bilateral contacts with Washington while refusing the regional coalition, citing fear of U.S. operations on Mexican soil. With the cartels being squeezed, three shifts are likely. WATCH: DHS ISSUES STARK WARNING AFTER 300 ‘HOSTILE’ CARTEL DRONES DETECTED AT SOUTHERN BORDER First, more "legitimate" business. Avocado orchards, fuel theft, mining extortion and chemical import fronts are already balance-sheet items. European logistics firms and real-estate laundering are the export version. Synthetics let production move to whatever jurisdiction still looks the other way. Second, sharper violence where territory is contested. Leadership disruption and route competition have historically produced spikes in ambushes, not quiet consolidation. Armored "monstruo" trucks, landmines and FPV drones lower the cost of killing rivals and local police. Expect more of it in Michoacán, Jalisco and the border plazas. TRUMP CAN PROTECT CALIFORNIA AVOCADO FARMERS AND TAKE A BITE OUT OF MEXICAN CARTELS, TOO Third, heavier investment in bribery and extortion of officials on both sides of the border. Lost geographic sanctuary makes a compromised port inspector, financial regulator or federal agent more valuable. This is old cartel practice. The premium on it rises when the political umbrellas fold. Latin America’s electoral realignment, the U.S. maritime campaign, the European meth seizures, the foreign-fighter drone pipeline and Mexico’s narrowing diplomatic company are enough. articles.title: The ‘world’s best bar’ for 2026 has been revealed
articles.summary: In our round-up of travel stories this week: why one US family moved from Virginia to Naples, how to stop a runaway plane, plus the verdict’s in on the world’s best bars, restaurants and hotels.
articles.body: In our round-up of travel stories this week: Why one US family moved from Virginia to Naples, how to stop a runaway plane, plus the verdict’s in on the world’s best bars, restaurants and hotels. The ‘world’s best bars’ When Lorenzo Antinori opened Bar Leone in Hong Kong’s fashionable Sheung Wan neighborhood in 2023, he wanted the Italian bar to feel “like my grandmother’s living room.” That mood is captured by the simple dark wood counter, the framed photos of everyone from Al Pacino to the pope, and the laid-back mid-century “dolce vita” feel – although not everyone’s nonna does such a delicious line in filthy martinis and olive oil sours. Bar Leone has for the second year running taken the No. 1 spot in the annual list of the world’s best bars put together by UK-based media company The 50. Its global academy of voters has anointed Milan’s Moebius Milano as the world’s No. 2 bar. Named for the sci-fi illustrator Moebius, it’s an avant-garde drinking spot in a former textile warehouse with a huge two-story-tall olive tree right in the center. At No. 3 is Alquímico, three stories of carnival-esque fun choreographed by an all-female bartending crew in a colonial building in the Colombian coastal city of Cartagena. The top 5 is rounded out by Bar Us in Bangkok (No. 4), a dimly lit “drinking room” that takes its cocktail flavors very seriously, and Line in Athens (No. 5), where drinks are fermented right on site. In recent years, The 50 has grown to become quite the list factory, turning out influential annual verdicts on the world’s best restaurant (Maido in Lima), hotel (Rosewood Hong Kong) and vineyard (Vik in Chile’s Millahue Valley). Those lists are mighty useful for publicists and for in-the-know travelers who love that zeitgeist zest – but, personally, my favorite bar of 2026 is an Irish pub in North London with a pool table, karaoke and 10 flavors of Baileys. Just follow the checklist in your heart. Back in old Napoli European countries such as Portugal and Spain are a popular choice for US expats. For the Salesberry family from Virginia, however, it was Italy that stole their heart. They moved to Naples sight unseen nine years ago and never looked back. “We had to learn the art of slowing down,” says Jason Salesberry of a local culture where restaurants rarely open for dinner before 7 p.m. and meals might last two or three hours. “Yet, the benefits have far outweighed the adjustments.” In the CNN series “Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy,” the actor visited Naples and the Amalfi coast to try the region’s famous pizza, search for the best San Marzano tomatoes and explore the volcanic island of Ischia. CNN subscribers can watch here. Aviation innovation Turkey’s record-breaking iGA Istanbul Airport has overtaken London Heathrow as the world’s best-connected airport, according to a new report by global travel data provider OAG. The huge megahub opened in 2018 and the site is bigger than the whole of Manhattan. Last month, it opened a fourth runway and CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN they’re just getting started. Read more about the airport’s ambitions. New innovations are also being introduced at US airports. articles.body: After sitting cold for more than 40 years, a Rhode Island murder case may have been solved with the recovery of a discarded water bottle in a theater. On Oct. 6, William "Billy" Morton was arrested and charged with first-degree murder for allegedly killing Hillary Hellewell in Newport in 1985. After four decades, investigators used new DNA technology that allegedly links 61-year-old Morton to the crime. DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON Since her death, investigators had slowly uncovered clues that suggested Morton might be a suspect. She was wearing white painter’s pants, a sweater, and socks but no shoes. Her pulseless body was mostly "cold to the touch," with some areas still "slightly warm" when officers arrived, Morton’s arrest warrant shows. articles.title: “These days, parents often react…”: Mahhi Vij on why overprotecting children can can affect their confidence; parenting lesson to take home
articles.summary: TV Actor and Bigg Boss 20 contestant Mahhi Vij has spoken about how the way parents respond to everyday childhood experiences can influence a child's
articles.body: TV Actor and Bigg Boss 20 contestant Mahhi Vij has spoken about how the way parents respond to everyday childhood experiences can influence a child's ability to handle situations independently. In a conversation with Hauterrfly, Mahhi recalled how her own parents encouraged her to get back up after a fall rather than rushing to protect her from every minor injury. She contrasted that experience with what she sees as a tendency among parents today to react immediately when a child gets hurt. “My parents were very carefree. If we fell down, they would tell us to get up on our own,” Mahhi said. “These days, parents often react immediately when a child falls. They rush to put a bandage on the injury and keep worrying about it. When children are overprotected, they may find it difficult to handle things on their own when they grow up and their parents are not around,” she added.Her comments came during a discussion about childhood confidence and the ways parents can help build it. The interviewer asked whether Mahhi's mother had done anything that helped her develop confidence, and whether, as a mother herself, she sometimes found herself repeating the parenting patterns she had grown up with. In her view, children also need opportunities to learn how to manage small difficulties themselves.Mahhi Vij recalls strict punishments from her childhoodMahhi's account of her childhood also included experiences that were far from carefree. She recalled being physically punished when she failed in mathematics and getting into trouble after her first school romance came to her parents' attention. “I still remember being beaten badly as a child. If I failed in maths, I would get beaten. I was also punished when my first school romance was discovered because the school called my parents,” she said. When asked why she had been punished over the relationship, Mahhi shared an incident from her school days. She said she was popular among boys in her school and neighbourhood, and that some boys would even break through the school fence to enter the canteen.“My boyfriend and some other boys got into a fight over me. Meanwhile, I would just be sitting in the canteen eating samosas. I didn’t even make eye contact with the boys,” she recalled. Mahhi also remembered Valentine's Day from that period, adding a humorous note to the story by imagining how her daughter might react if she watched the interview in the future. “If my daughter watches this interview one day, she will tell me, ‘Mumma, if I get that kind of attention, you must not say anything!’” she said.What parents can do to build independence without ignoring a child's needsMahhi's comments raise a practical question for parents: when should they step in, and when should they allow a child to try handling a situation independently? The answer depends on the situation. A child who trips on a flat surface but is not seriously hurt may benefit from being given a moment to get up, check how they feel and decide what they need. A child who is injured, frightened or in danger, however, needs an adult's attention and help. Encouraging independence does not mean ignoring pain or refusing comfort.Here are three ways parents can help children practise handling everyday setbacks:Pause before rushing in: If a child has a minor fall or makes a small mistake, first check whether they are safe. Instead of immediately doing everything for them, ask, “Are you hurt? What do you think you should do?” This gives them a chance to assess the situation while knowing an adult is nearby.Let children take the first step towards solving a problem: If a child forgets a school item, struggles with a simple task or has a disagreement with a friend, resist the urge to fix everything immediately. Ask what they have tried and what they could do next. Step in when the problem is beyond their ability or when they need protection.Separate mistakes from a child's worth: Mahhi recalled being beaten when she failed in mathematics. Parents can respond differently by focusing on what went wrong and what could help next time. For example, instead of reacting angrily to a poor test score, they can ask which topics the child found difficult and help make a plan to practise them.Children do not become independent simply because adults leave them to manage everything alone. They need a balance: room to try, permission to make age-appropriate mistakes and reassurance that help is available when they need it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Jharkhand’s first grain ATM in Jamshedpur, to become functional after Durga Puja
articles.summary: Jharkhand’s first grain ATM in Jamshedpur to go live after Durga Puja, letting ration cardholders use biometrics to dispense wheat or rice; more planned in Ranchi, Dhanbad.
articles.body: Jamshedpur: Jharkhand’s first automated food grain dispensing machine will become functional in Jamshedpur after Durga Puja, officials here said.Popularly known as Annapurti ATM, the automated dispenser has been set up in the block-cum-circle office in Parsudih’s Khasmahal, and its trial runs are currently underway. Technical teams are assessing its performance, including dispensing speed and operation during power outages using battery backup before formal launch.“A preliminary trial has been conducted. Further testing will continue over the next few days before the launch,” Jamshedpur block development officer (BDO) Sumit Prakash said. A power backup is being put in place to keep the facility functional during power cuts.The grain ATMs will allow ration cardholders to authenticate themselves through a biometric scanner after entering their registered mobile number. Beneficiaries can then select wheat or rice through a touchscreen interface, and the allotted quantity will be dispensed directly into their bags. The entire process is expected to take around 10 minutes.Ration cardholders from any part of East Singhbhum district can access it.The Annapurti ATM is part of a Centre-backed initiative under the World Food Programme aimed at improving transparency and convenience in the public distribution system. Thirty-two such machines have been installed across the country. In Jharkhand, two other grain ATMs are proposed in Ranchi and Dhanbad.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Isaias brings flood, tornado threats across US Southeast after Florida landfall
articles.summary: By Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Pardesi Oct 10 (Reuters) - Isaias is expected to bring storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes...
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias expected to make landfall on US gulf coast

By Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Pardesi

Oct 10 (Reuters) - Isaias is expected to bring storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk ‌of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast on Saturday, even as ‌the storm weakens after making landfall in Florida, the National Hurricane Center said.

The center warned of ​considerable impacts across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.

The tornado threat will continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said.

Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone on Saturday, ‌having rapidly lost wind speed ⁠after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, the NHC said ⁠in its latest advisory.

Isaias is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said.

Alabama's emergency management agency ​said ​the hurricane has downed trees and power ​lines, making travel hazardous in Houston ‌County, which is under a flash flood warning.

"Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. "These road closures will remain in effect until conditions are deemed safe for travel."

President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations, told reporters outside the White House, "We're ‌watching it very closely, the hurricane," adding ​that it was "under control."

More than 430,000 customers in ​Florida and nearly 297,000 in ​Alabama lost power as the storm hit shore, according to ‌power outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.

"Emergency declarations have ​been approved in ​Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.

Florida's emergency services urged ​residents to shelter in ‌place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of the ​state.

(Reporting by Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Singh Pardesi in Bengaluru; ​Editing by William Mallard and Ros Russell)

articles.title: Police detain dozens and check 50,000 schools after two attacks shake Poland
articles.summary: Police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week.
articles.body: Police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week. On Friday, schools across Poland stepped up security, with some suspending classes, many parents keeping children at home and police patrols deployed to educational institutions after two attacks at schools earlier in the week left one person dead and several others wounded, including children. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the Mazovian province in central Poland attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing and being arrested nearby. The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two others in a knife attack at his former school in the same province. The assaults, both carried out by Polish nationals, shocked a country where school violence by minors is a new phenomenon. By Thursday night, rumours that the attacks were coordinated and that there would be more on the culmination day dubbed “bloody Friday” were being shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media. Fifty-nine schools preemptively suspended classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in the Mazovian district, where the capital Warsaw is located. School directors sent messages announcing stepped-up security measures including extra school staff placed at entrances and voluntary backpack checks. “There will ⁠be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said. Those detained on Friday include a 14-year-old boy from a central district of Warsaw who was found in possession of a knife with a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers, and a 16-year old from another Warsaw district who came to school with a butterfly knife in his backpack. Others had posted online photos of knives, threatened their peers or threatened school attacks. So far, the government said, it had found no evidence that an internet challenge promoting school attacks was ongoing. There is also no official confirmation that the two attacks were linked; both perpetrators are in custody. Parents across Poland are now having to catch up fast on how to speak to their kids about school violence. Authorities say extra security measures at schools will continue and crisis training will be organized. The liberal government also promised to renew efforts to pass a bill blocking harmful online content. “If that juvenile attacker had streamed the crime online today, we would have been unable to block that content because we have not been given that legal tool,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. After wounding three adults in Thursday’s attack, the 15-year-old, who wore a camera to record his actions, was eventually overpowered by school director Krzysztof Ochmański. Ochmański later told reporters there was a moment when the boy seemed to realise the enormity of his actions and said he did not want to do this any more. “Once I had established contact, he asked me for help,” Ochmański recounted. “It got to the point where he wanted a hug.”

articles.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
articles.summary: Former students launched their own investigation, spending years collecting evidence and testimonies from others who say they were abused by the headteacher.
articles.body:
A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.

Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.

Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him , and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.

The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.

Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault

Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube .

Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.

They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.

By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.

Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.

Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.

Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.

In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.

"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.

Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.

In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.

Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.

Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".

The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.

The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.

One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.

"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."

Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married , were overwhelmed by the response from former students.

"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."

Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.

"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.

Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.

"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.

Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.

The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.

NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.

In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.
